Rather than reading secular books to select for official office, why not study the supramundane Dharma to select for Buddhahood? The Master approved of his words and resolutely desired to transcend the mundane world.

However, while sitting alone to care for his mother, he harbored his intention but did not dare to voice it; he remained in a state of deep melancholy, as if he had lost something. His mother found this strange and questioned him.
He explained his reasons in detail, and [his mother] found it quite difficult to accept. The Master then recited a verse, saying: "The *huángzhōng* note is sung to its full pitch;
the *dàshí* mode is blown to perfection. For ten thousand ages no one has been a true connoisseur; a donkey chooses a damp spot to urinate.

His mother, realizing that his resolve could not be swayed, went at once to appeal to her father. Her grandfather supported her decision, enabling him to pay respects to Master Jiàn, receive the tonsure, and ascend to the stage of full ordination.
While traveling, he first met Ying’an Hua at Tiantong, but their karmic conditions did not harmonize. He returned to Jingci Temple and relied upon Yuetang Chang.

Zhixu-deng sighed and said: "The Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs permeates all things and is widely diffused;

Although you claim to have 'continued' [the lineage], it is as if your illumination were not universal. Why is this so? You ought to collect those omissions."
The one who possessed the complete eye of the school’s essential tenets brought it to perfection; thus, the work of *Pǔdēng* (Universal Lamp) was inaugurated.
He subsequently visited Wú'ān Quán at Dàodichǎng and Xiètáng Yuǎn at Hùqīu. When Rén'táng resided at Zhōngzhú, he invited [Wǔfǎ] to serve as his head disciple (*shàngshǒu*).

Not long after, he returned to his hometown. At Zhēnchá, Lǐwànhuà of Wànshòu Monastery met him upon first sight and found they were in perfect accord, and thus he was commissioned [to lead the monastery].

When [the Master] was invited to share his seat and preach the Dharma, the Master looked upon him with disdain. At the beginning of the Qingyuan era, he traveled by boat through the Shai River to the capital, where he stayed at the Shouxing Monastery on the lake;
thereafter, he withdrew in seclusion to his mountain retreat, remaining aloof from worldly contact. I, Yu, was then fortunate enough to have the opportunity to serve as his disciple.

He immediately advanced to request further instruction, saying privately: "I have heard that when Bodhidharma came from the West, he pointed directly at the human mind, seeing one's nature as becoming a Buddha, and did not establish reliance on written words.
Yet, when transmitting the Dharma to the Second Patriarch, he bestowed the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* to serve as a seal of the Buddha-mind.

How can this be anything other than written words? I pray you will dispel my confusion. The Master gave him skillful instruction, and his doubts were melted away like ice. Thereupon, [the student] spoke of this sutra.

The contents were profound and abstruse; even readers could not yet parse the individual phrases. [The Master] was requested to provide an exegesis for the benefit of future students, and it was decided that the work should be carved into printing blocks.
The Master then joyfully expounded upon the meanings and principles. Furthermore, based on Jiyin’s *Lengyan* commentary, he revised, supplemented, and expanded it into a comprehensive treatise.

Seventeen scrolls were transcribed and bound together, and he presented them to the imperial court. All three works were subsequently carved onto printing blocks and circulated throughout the world.

Master Li (Li Tongxuan) further expanded upon it with his commentaries, which are so voluminous in text and profound in meaning that few are able to recite them from beginning to end. The Master [Huiyuan] therefore extracted the essentials and summarized the core points, pruning away all superfluous length.
He synthesized eighty fascicles of sutras and forty fascicles of treatises into three volumes;

the language was concise yet the principles reached their ultimate depth, as if they were held in the palm of one's hand. All received his instruction. By nature, the Master was pure and profound, with exceptional insight and vision.

With the aim of expounding the teachings and propagating the fundamental tenets, he rejected fame and profit; thus, he repeatedly declined invitations from renowned monasteries before finally withdrawing into seclusion.
Jiezang kept his practices secret. Dwelling in a hermitage on the outskirts of the city, he manifested a slight illness in the first year of the Jiading era, the year of Wuchen (1208).

He was sixty-three years of age and forty-seven years since his ordination.

It is like a tripod supported by its legs; if one leg falters, the tripod overturns. I have long admired those men and examined their teachings, whereby I came to know that the essence of the Confucian teaching lies in sincerity of intention (*chengyi*);
the essence of the Daoist teaching lies in the emptying of the mind (*xuxin*);

and the essence of the Buddhist teaching lies in the realization of nature (*jianxing*). Sincerity of intention, emptying of the mind, and realization of nature—though they have different names, they share the same substance.

Investigating their ultimate refuge, there is nowhere that does not converge with this Way. Sages and enlightened kings transmitted it to one another through "purity and unity," embodying it in profound silence and personal practice;
how could they have looked outside of this? Is it not because their wisdom was perfect and their understanding of words complete?
Nevertheless, regarding the Buddhist Way of realizing the nature, beyond what is expounded in the Tripitaka, the Tathāgata further established the Dharma of the "One Mind" of the former Buddhas.
[The seal] was entrusted to Upagupta. From Upagupta down to Dharmatrāta, there were twenty-eight transmissions in total.

Like a lamp transmitting its light, their radiance continues one after another. Thus, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* (Fu fazang zhuan) says: "By means of this lamp of wisdom, it is transmitted in succession."
Since the time of Bodhidharma, this lamp has divided its radiance to shine far and wide; even Buddhas and patriarchs cannot obscure it, nor can they conceal it.
Because it cannot be obscured or concealed, those individuals are often called "transmitters" (liutong), and their words are called "dhāraṇīs" (zongchi).
Regarding the term *dhāraṇī*, there is a distinction between that of the Buddhas and that of the patriarchs. Speaking from the perspective of the Buddhas:

The profound intent of the various patriarchs is clearly and fully revealed within the jeweled cases of the Dragon Canon; this is precisely what is meant by the "Three Lamps. Recently, while serving under Chan Master Fuxing Daochang of Jingci, he pointed to the *Continued Record of the Lamp* one day and sighed, saying to me: "The three types of grass and two types of trees differ from one another, yet when they receive the moisture, they are one and the same. As for what he said: [...text omitted... ...it is as stated therein. It is not that the Buddhas and patriarchs have ever been separate from the Way;

it is simply that they have manifested the Way according to the capacities of sentient beings. Therefore, the Great Master [Bodhidharma] came from the West, and the Sixth Patriarch transmitted the seal of mind. From the time of the Second Patriarch down to the present, there has been no deviation from the original source. Although the teachings of the various schools may appear different, their ultimate aim is to enable practitioners to realize the Buddha-nature within themselves. This is why the *Record of the Lamp* was compiled—to ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas and patriarchs would not be interrupted. If one does not rely on these records, how can one discern the true transmission? Thus, the Three Lamps serve as the standard for verifying the succession of the Dharma.

To study the Buddhas and patriarchs without relying on the lamp records is like trying to find one’s way in the dark without a torch; it is impossible to avoid error. Therefore, those who wish to enter the gate of the Buddhas and patriarchs must first consult the lamp records. Once one has understood the lamp records, one will naturally see that the essence of the Way is originally complete and perfect, requiring neither addition nor subtraction. This is the very meaning of the "Three Lamps. May you take this to heart and propagate it widely. Do not let the lamp of the Buddhas and patriarchs go out. This is my earnest exhortation. Though I hesitated and withdrew time and again, I have nonetheless taken refuge among the thickets at the mountain’s edge to venture this humble offering to Your Majesty. I still hope it may be promulgated to benefit the religious tradition;

The Song of Silent Meditation (with Preface): Chan Master Wushan Shizi’s “Sleeping Words” and “Song of Letting the Cattle Loose” **Preface** Chan Master Wushan Shizi was a man of great realization who lived during the late Yuan dynasty. He was known for his profound silence and his ability to express the ultimate through the ordinary. This collection contains his "Sleeping Words," which he composed while resting in the midst of his practice, and his "Song of Letting the Cattle Loose," a spontaneous expression of his liberation. Together, these works reveal the seamless integration of daily life and the Way, demonstrating how the mundane and the sacred are one and the same. **Sleeping Words** When the sun sets and the moon rises, I lie down upon my mat. No need to seek the Buddha or the patriarchs; Just this very moment is the true state. If you wish to understand the ancient sages, Look directly at your own face before birth. When the dream ends and the sleep is over, The vast expanse is naturally clear and bright. **Song of Letting the Cattle Loose** The great ox has been let loose; He roams freely across the ten directions. He does not follow the tracks of the old masters, Nor does he stay within the boundaries of the scriptures. Sometimes he grazes on the clouds and mist, Sometimes he drinks from the rivers and seas. He knows no fear of the tiger’s cave, And he is unafraid of the lion’s den. When hunger comes, he eats the grass of the wild fields; When thirst arises, he drinks from the spring of the source. He is neither bound by the rope of discipline, Nor constrained by the tether of wisdom. In the end, he returns to the place of origin, Where the horns of the ox are lost in the void. This is the song of letting the cattle loose— A free and easy wandering in the realm of the Great Function.

Song of Begging Sent to Chan Master Ya for His Journey to Shicheng; Chanting Master Zhao of Baofeng Composes a Song in the Style of Minister Lu Dexian’s “Song of Inscription on Disciples. *Quantu ming* (Inscription on Disciples) I have heard that the Great Way is vast and boundless, Yet people cling to narrow paths and refuse to turn back. If one does not abandon the world and depart from it, How can one escape the cycle of birth and death? The Buddha appeared in the world to save sentient beings; His teachings are like a great bridge spanning the ocean of suffering. If you do not cross this bridge while there is still time, When will you ever find the opportunity to do so? The Dharma-body is originally pure and free from defilement; It is the true nature of all phenomena, beyond conceptualization. To seek it through words and letters is to wander further astray; Only by cutting off all thoughts can one realize it. Do not be attached to forms or appearances; Seek only the mind-ground within yourself. If you can realize this for yourself, You will know that the Buddhas of the three times are all within.

I urge my disciples to practice with diligence; Do not let the years pass in vain. If you can maintain this resolve until the end, You will surely attain the fruit of liberation. May you all cultivate yourselves with earnestness, And together reach the shore of Nirvana. This song is written as an exhortation; May it serve as a lasting reminder for all.
